lessons.title: Effects and External Synchronization
lessons.summary: Effects synchronize React with systems outside React: subscriptions, browser APIs, imperative widgets, manual network work.
lessons.body:
Effects and External Synchronization

Why this matters
Effects synchronize React with systems outside React: subscriptions, browser APIs, imperative widgets, manual network work. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Effects synchronize React with systems outside React: subscriptions, browser APIs, imperative widgets, manual network work.
• An effect is not needed to calculate a value from props/state.
• Dependencies describe values used by the effect; suppressing dependency warnings can hide stale closures.
• Cleanup should undo subscriptions/timers/imperative resources from the previous effect instance.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, react foundations ii stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter effects and external synchronization again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: Refs and Imperative Escape Hatches
lessons.summary: Refs hold mutable values that do not trigger rendering and can reference DOM nodes.
lessons.body:
Refs and Imperative Escape Hatches

Why this matters
Refs hold mutable values that do not trigger rendering and can reference DOM nodes. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

• Refs hold mutable values that do not trigger rendering and can reference DOM nodes.
• Use refs for focus, measurement, integration with imperative libraries, or instance-like values.

lessons.title: Context and Provider Boundaries
lessons.summary: Context passes a value through a subtree without threading props through every intermediate component.
lessons.body:
Context and Provider Boundaries

Why this matters
Context passes a value through a subtree without threading props through every intermediate component. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Context passes a value through a subtree without threading props through every intermediate component.
• It does not automatically make state global, performant, or suitable for server data.
• Provider placement controls which subtree re-renders when the context value identity changes.
• Use context for stable cross-cutting dependencies/state when it fits, not as the default state container.

lessons.title: Reducers for Explicit State Transitions
lessons.summary: useReducer is useful when local state has several related transitions and named events improve clarity.
lessons.body:
Reducers for Explicit State Transitions

Why this matters
useReducer is useful when local state has several related transitions and named events improve clarity. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• useReducer is useful when local state has several related transitions and named events improve clarity.

lessons.title: React Debugging and Render Reasoning
lessons.summary: When UI is wrong, identify the source of truth and inspect props/state at the render where the problem occurs.
lessons.body:
React Debugging and Render Reasoning

Why this matters
When UI is wrong, identify the source of truth and inspect props/state at the render where the problem occurs. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• When UI is wrong, identify the source of truth and inspect props/state at the render where the problem occurs.
• React DevTools can show component tree and values, but first reason about ownership and identity.
• Unexpected repeated effects often indicate unstable dependencies or development Strict Mode behavior, not necessarily a framework bug.
• Reduce the component to a minimal reproduction when state ownership is unclear.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, react foundations ii stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter react debugging and render reasoning again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.body:
Lab: React Debugging and Render Reasoning

Purpose
This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Build the smallest runnable example for “React Debugging and Render Reasoning”, predict its output, change one assumption, and explain the difference using concrete evidence.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

Definition of done
You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.
